title: How Russia Is Attacking the Midterms with a Mother Jones Deepfake

reading.body:
This is a synthetic media impersonation, not a model error. A fabricated video was produced to look like the work of an established news outlet, using invented footage of that outlet's editor-in-chief, and it was distributed through social media accounts rather than published on any real news site. The false claim at its centre, that a political party paid a broadcaster's executive to promote gender transition in children, was presented as documented fact and attributed to hacked emails.

The failure sits at the point of distribution, not generation. The video carried a real outlet's branding and a real person's likeness, which is what gave the fabricated claim its apparent authority, and the platform hosting it had no check in place before it accumulated views. Catching it would have required verifying the branded source against the outlet itself, or a platform-side check on synthetic media impersonating a named publisher before amplification, and neither happened until the outlet complained.

What the reporting establishes is that the video was removed for a trademark violation after that complaint, and that researchers assessed the accounts as showing bot-like signs with likely inflated view counts. It is not established that the operation succeeded in changing anyone's beliefs, and the article's own assessment is that the campaign had not gone viral. The attribution of the operation to a Russian network and its stated aim of aiding one party rest on researcher assessment, not on any finding presented in the reporting.

reports.title: How Russia Is Attacking the Midterms with a Mother Jones Deepfake

summary:
A Russian disinformation network known as Storm-1679 or Matryoshka circulated a fake video falsely branded as Mother Jones. The video claimed the Democratic National Committee paid $259 million to CNN chief Mark Thompson to promote gender transition among children, citing emails supposedly hacked by Anonymous. It used fake footage of Mother Jones editor-in-chief Clara Jeffery and drew 155,000 views on one X account and 50,000 on another within a day. Researchers say the accounts showed bot-like signs and the views were likely inflated.

The operation is part of a Russian effort to influence the 2026 midterms and help Republicans. Matryoshka has also spread deepfakes of celebrities and fake reports impersonating major outlets. After Mother Jones complained, X removed the video for violating its trademark policy. The article says the campaign has not yet gone viral, but warns that Trump administration cuts to federal disinformation-tracking units leave the US more exposed.
title_en: How Russia Is Attacking the Midterms with a Mother Jones Deepfake
